title: Software for multi-omics data integration and analysis: a systematic and critical comparison of frameworks, packages, workflows and platforms, with EasyMultiProfiler as a featured workflow for microbiome research

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: the multi-omics integration imperative and the software gap
sections.goal: Establish why multi-omics integration demands purpose-built software rather than ad-hoc concatenation of single-omics pipelines. Open with the breadth of contemporary host-microbiome studies spanning pulmonary, cardiovascular, neurodevelopmental, oncological and neurodegenerative disease to argue that integration is no longer optional, then pivot to the operational reality: most published studies still treat 'multi-omics' as a label for parallel rather than joint analysis. Use the featured workflow EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) [R1] as the framing example of a workflow that responds to this gap, while critically noting that its emergence also signals how fragmented the prior ecosystem was.

sections.heading: 2. A taxonomy of integration strategies: unsupervised, supervised, and the longitudinal dimension
sections.goal: Provide a critical conceptual map of integration strategies (early concatenation, intermediate joint dimensionality reduction, late fusion/correlation) and the unsupervised–supervised axis. Emphasize that the field lacks consensus terminology and that seemingly distinct methods often share statistical underpinnings. Use timeOmics [R4] to illustrate the intermediate/clustering paradigm and the IBS longitudinal study [R12] to show why a temporal axis breaks most static integration approaches, thereby motivating workflow designs that explicitly accommodate time.

sections.heading: 3. General-purpose integration frameworks: timeOmics and the Bioconductor ecosystem
sections.goal: Survey general-purpose R/Bioconductor integration frameworks, anchored by timeOmics [R4] as a concrete example, and situate them within the broader ecosystem (MOFA, mixOmics, MultiAssayExperiment-backed tools). The critical angle: these packages are statistically rigorous but assume clean, dense, model-organism-style matrices and rarely handle the compositionality, zero-inflation and phylogenetic structure that characterise microbiome layers, which limits their usefulness for the host-microbiome community without substantial wrapper code.

sections.heading: 4. Microbiome-centred multi-omics tools and the heterogeneous application landscape
sections.goal: Catalogue the de facto microbiome multi-omics tooling by examining representative application studies rather than dedicated packages, because the latter remain scarce. Use the cross-cohort IBD integration [R10] as the closest example to a reproducible, reproducible framework, and the IBS profiling [R11] and longitudinal IBS study [R12] as exemplars of bespoke pipelines. The critical angle is that the microbiome community currently relies on investigator-built scripts stitched from phyloseq, vegan, mixOmics and individual omics layers, with little shared infrastructure — a gap that EMP [R1] explicitly aims to fill.

sections.heading: 5. Web servers and point-and-click platforms: accessibility versus scalability
sections.goal: Critically evaluate graphical multi-omics platforms, anchored by the Analyst suite (ExpressAnalyst, MetaboAnalyst, OmicsNet, OmicsAnalyst) [R3], which bundles single-omics analysis, knowledge-driven network integration and data-driven joint dimensionality reduction. Praise their role in democratising analysis for non-programmers and standardising preprocessing, but emphasise sharp limitations: upload-size ceilings that preclude modern cohort-scale microbiome data, limited support for compositional/zero-inflated microbiome tables, and restricted extensibility that locks users into upstream choices made by the platform developers.

sections.heading: 6. Data structures, workflow systems and reproducibility
sections.goal: Analyse how container data structures (SummarizedExperiment, MultiAssayExperiment, TreeSummarizedExperiment) and pipeline frameworks underpin reproducibility in modern multi-omics software. EMP [R1] is a paradigmatic example, organising extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation modules around these classes. Critically argue that adopting a standard container is necessary but not sufficient: version pinning, container images, controlled vocabularies and provenance metadata are equally required, and even EMP [R1] does not yet provide a fully containerised execution environment comparable to nf-core-style workflows.

sections.heading: 7. Benchmarking evidence and evaluation criteria
sections.goal: Establish what credible evaluation of integration software looks like, foregrounding SUMO [R2] as the only widely available simulator of multi-omics data with user-defined latent structure, noise and complexity. Use the IBD cross-cohort biomarker analysis [R10] as an empirical benchmark of cross-study robustness. The critical angle: most integration tools are evaluated on a single dataset by their authors; cross-tool, cross-dataset benchmarks using simulators like SUMO [R2] remain rare, and reported performance is therefore dataset- and preprocessing-dependent rather than generalisable.

sections.heading: 8. EasyMultiProfiler: a focused workflow for microbiome multi-omics
sections.goal: Deliver the dedicated, balanced evaluation of EMP [R1] mandated by the review. Articulate its design rationale (SummarizedExperiment/MultiAssayExperiment backbone; five-module architecture spanning extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation; natural-language-style pipeline interface) and its comparative advantages over general frameworks [R4], web platforms [R3] and bespoke application pipelines [R11, R12]: native handling of microbiome-specific objects, end-to-end coverage and reproducibility hooks. Equally candidly state its limitations: scope restricted to microbiome-centric host-microbe studies, dependence on a maturing R/Bioconductor stack, no native simulation capability (cf. SUMO [R2]), and the absence so far of large independent benchmark studies analogous to [R10].

sections.heading: 9. Critical perspectives: heterogeneity, hype and the limits of integration
sections.goal: Interrogate the field's claims through a critical lens using the disease-specific application studies as evidence. Show that even methodologically careful multi-omics studies in IPF [R5], atherosclerosis [R6], autism [R7], glioma [R8] and Alzheimer's disease [R9] reach partly inconsistent and context-dependent conclusions about which microbial features matter, and that even IBS — a closer-to-microbiome-centric disease — yields classifier outputs whose generalisability across subtypes remains contested [R11, R12]. The critical angle: software cannot rescue biological heterogeneity, and integration methods that ignore compositional bias, confounders and cross-cohort batch effects will continue to produce irreproducible 'signatures' regardless of algorithmic sophistication.

sections.heading: 10. Recommendations for users and developers, and outlook
sections.goal: Translate the comparative survey into actionable guidance. For users: match tool choice to data scale (web suites [R3] for small exploratory cohorts; EMP [R1] for microbiome-centric workflows; SUMO [R2] for simulation-led method development; longitudinal-aware packages [R4] for time-series; cross-cohort frameworks [R10] when generalisability is the goal). For developers: prioritise simulation-driven benchmarking [R2], standard containers [R1], cross-cohort validation [R10], and explicit handling of compositional and zero-inflated data, since the application literature [R5–R9, R11, R12] shows that biological, not algorithmic, heterogeneity is currently the dominant source of irreproducibility. Conclude by positioning EMP [R1] as an important community step rather than a finished solution.
